newsitem.title: ITALY: Italy MPs in revolt against Prodi on unemployment.
newsitem.headline: Italy MPs in revolt against Prodi on unemployment.

text.p: Prime Minister Romano Prodi has touched off a storm of protest, not only among the opposition but also from within his coalition, by accusing parliament of dragging its feet on measures to boost employment.

"Parliament in revolt against Prodi," was the identical headline both Milan's Corriere Della Sera and Turin's La Stampa newspapers used on Tuesday to describe the burning political atmosphere created by Prodi's remarks.

Prodi, speaking after President Oscar Luigi Scalfaro expressed concern about Italy's jobless rate, on Sunday accused parliament of moving slowly to enact legislation that would help lower unemployment, currently at more than 12 percent.
His remarks prompted a barrage of criticism from parliamentarians across the political spectrum and demands for a clarification.

The speakers of the Senate and Chamber of Deputies demanded a meeting with Prodi on Thursday after he returns from a trip to Poland and Slovenia. Prodi has made no comment yet on the controversy back home.
Underscoring the sensitivity of the unemployment issue, even the centre-left parties that make up his coalition did not spare their criticism.

Senator Cesare Salvi of the Democratic Party of the Left (PDS), the backbone of the coalition, said it was "grotesque" that Prodi tried to blame parliament for delays that were "completely and exclusively attributable to the government".
"To assert that delays in unemployment provisions are the fault of parliament is devoid of any foundation," Salvi said.
"Whipping parliament (over unemployment) without being specific is wrong," said Fabio Mussi, the PDS leader in the lower house.
Another leading PDS parliamentarian, Pietro Folena, urged Prodi to think before he speaks.
It was some of the stiffest criticism Prodi has faced from within his own coalition since his centre-left government took office last May.

Opposition Senator Enrico La Loggia of Silvio Berlusconi's Forza Italia party said Prodi "must be suffering from a serious nervous breakdown ... because he doesn't know how to distinguish between the duties of the government and those of parliament".
On another issue, Prodi also faced a near-ultimatum from Foreign Minister Lamberto Dini over the coalition's relations with the hard-left Communist Refoundation party.
Dini, a former prime minister and central banker who heads the centrist Italian Renewal party, said in a interview published on Tuesday that the coalition should not "abuse my sense of loyalty".
Some coalition partners have been uneasy from the time the government was formed over Prodi's relations with Communist Refoundation, on which it relies for its majority in the lower house.

"I have already shouted several times. Prodi cannot always sell us agreement already worked out with Refoundation. They must be careful not to abuse my sense of loyalty. There can be some surprises," Dini told the Il Foglio newspaper.

Centrist coalition partners have expressed discomfort with what they see as attempts by Prodi to accommodate Communist Refoundation leader Fausto Bertinotti on issues such as pensions, health and welfare issues.
